name: french lentil salad
instructions:
Two variants now: VARIANT A is the COLD SIDE — sautéed leeks + raw endives + cold lentils in the cream vinaigrette. VARIANT B is a HOT MAIN — lentils mashed with a dauphinois (cream and all) plus some vinegar, skipping the vegetables. French parsley is good in both versions.

=== THE CREAM VINAIGRETTE (VARIANT A) ===

Whisk heavy cream, white wine vinegar, dijon mustard, and raw minced garlic together. Both the vinegar and the mustard go in — mustard adds savory depth and helps emulsify, vinegar carries the sharp french-vinaigrette acid. Neither alone is enough. NO LEMON — clashing; the VINEGAR + CREAM combo is the point (see notes).

=== VARIANT A — COLD SIDE (SAUTÉED LEEKS + RAW ENDIVES) ===

1. SAUTÉ LEEKS in olive oil over medium heat until softened — this is the ONLY place olive oil appears in the recipe (see notes). Optionally deglaze with a splash of white wine and let it cook off. Cool.
2. In a bowl, combine COLD cooked lentils with RAW ENDIVES (strongly preferred; radishes are the backup — one french vegetable only, never two).
3. Fold in the cooled leeks. Pour the cream vinaigrette over and toss.
4. Fold in chopped fresh parsley (non-optional).

=== VARIANT B — HOT MAIN (LENTILS MASHED WITH DAUPHINOIS) ===

1. Make a [[dauphinois]] — a TURNIP-HEAVY dauphinois is the recommendation, but potatoes are okay too.
2. MASH the plain cooked lentils with the dauphinois — CREAM AND ALL. NO VINEGAR — I suspect it's unnecessary here; the hot cream carries the variant (see THE REAL SPLIT note).
3. The dauphinois is the vegetable — no endives, no leeks (see THE REAL SPLIT note).
4. Parsley is good here too. Serve hot as a main.
notes:
THE STRUCTURE (variant A): cold lentils + cream vinaigrette (cream + mustard + vinegar + garlic) + raw endives + sautéed leeks + parsley. Variant B trades the salad format for a hot mash: lentils + dauphinois + vinegar.

NON-FLEXIBLE (variant A rules):
- LENTILS COOKED AND COLD (NOT IN THE PAN): the lentils never enter the sauté pan. Adding them to the pan is the trap — once they get mushy and heated, they start demanding stock, tarragon, and other stew-like vegetables, and the raw french vegetable and vinaigrette will clash with that direction. (Variant B is where the hot-lentil urge goes — it commits fully, with the dauphinois carrying it.)
- CREAM + MUSTARD + VINEGAR + GARLIC IN THE VINAIGRETTE: all four are primary.
- ENDIVES: strongly preferred — load-bearing.
- PARSLEY: non-optional in both variants.

=== NO LEMON — VINEGAR + CREAM IS THE POINT ===

LEMON IS CLASHING in this recipe and in the cream vinaigrette specifically. The VINEGAR + CREAM combination is the point of the dressing — lemon's acid is a different register and undermines it.

=== CREAM VINAIGRETTE — MUSTARD AND VINEGAR BOTH, NOT PICK-ONE ===

The dressing is heavy cream + white wine vinegar + dijon mustard + raw minced garlic. Both the vinegar and the mustard are primary — neither alone is enough. Mustard on its own reads too round-and-savory and loses the sharp french-vinaigrette acid; vinegar on its own reads too sharp without the mustard's emulsifying, depth-adding backbone. Together they lock the dressing into the right register.

White wine (the actual wine) is secondary — a nice deglaze for the leek sauté but not what the dressing is built on.

GARLIC ALWAYS RAW IN THE VINAIGRETTE.

=== OLIVE OIL — LEEK SAUTÉ ONLY ===

The ONLY place olive oil should appear in this recipe is sautéing the leeks. It's not a dressing component and not a finishing drizzle — the cream + vinegar + mustard is the fat-and-acid backbone. This is also the fix for the dish's main failure mode: a soggy, oil-heavy salad is almost always too much olive oil (over-oiled leeks or a finishing drizzle). Minimum required for the sauté, nothing more.

=== ENDIVES + PARSLEY ARE LOAD-BEARING (ENDIVES SPECIFICALLY RAW) ===

Variant A's identity — bitter-crunchy-green cold lentil salad in a sharp cream vinaigrette — sits on endives + parsley specifically. Endives give the RAW crunchy-bitter-nutty body that reads distinctly french and stands up to the cream; parsley gives the raw green herbaceous backbone that keeps the cream from reading flat.

ENDIVES ARE SPECIFICALLY RAW — DON'T COOK THEM: cooking endives strips the specific nuttiness and crunch that makes them fit this salad; cooked they read as generic braised greens.

FRENCH VEGETABLE — pick ONE, never more: endives (strongly preferred) or radishes (backup). These are bitter vegetables — the cream can balance one bitter element, not two.

RAW TURNIPS TRIED — DIDN'T LAND: bitterness reads muddy against the cream vinaigrette rather than crisp-bitter like endives, and raw turnip lacks the wafer-crunch. (The cooked-turnip direction graduated into VARIANT B — the turnip-heavy dauphinois mash.)

PARSLEY IS THE HERB — NOT TARRAGON, NOT MINT: tarragon pushes toward a stew-lentil register; mint reads middle-eastern. Parsley sits cleanly under the cream in both variants.

=== VARIANT B — WHERE THE DAUPHINOIS EXPERIMENT LANDED ===

The old want-to-try (dauphinois-style cream-braised turnip + potato folded into the salad) became its own variant: mash plain cooked lentils with a dauphinois, cream and all. TURNIP-HEAVY dauphinois recommended; potatoes okay too. It's a hot main, not a salad with cooked add-ins.

=== THE REAL SPLIT — PRELIMINARY ASSESSMENT ===

I suspect the vinegar is unnecessary in the hot version. Preliminary assessment of the split:
- VARIANT A (cold): VINEGAR, ENDIVES, AND LEEKS in — the bright/bitter/allium axis.
- VARIANT B (hot): NONE of them — just the SPICED DAUPHINOIS (the savory axis; [[dauphinois]] brings its nutmeg + white pepper + allspice).

(An earlier idea — raw endives riding into the hot version — is off the table under this assessment; endives stay cold-side.)

=== WANT TO TRY — FENNEL DIRECTIONS (VARIANT A) ===

1. RAW FENNEL in the endive/radish slot (not alongside). Anise-forward crunch; slightly more mediterranean than french. Untested.
2. LIGHTLY SAUTÉED FENNEL BULB — mellower anise, softer texture, comparable in cook-treatment to the leeks. Untested.

Endives is the tested working pick; fennel is the challenger.
